summary: Dual-Stack Lite gives customers with only an IPv6 prefix both IPv4 and IPv6 connectivity, but the B4 element needs the address of the AFTR tunnel endpoint. This RFC defines RADIUS extensions so that information can be stored in AAA profiles and delivered to the customer equipment.

eli5.summary: Some homes only have the new kind of internet address but still want to visit old sites. This lets the provider's records tell the home router where to find the helper that makes that work.

questions: how does b4 learn the aftr
what is the ds-lite-tunnel-name radius attribute
how does a b4 learn the aftr name
subtitle: A RADIUS attribute that hands a home gateway's tunnel endpoint name from the provider's AAA server to the access server.

tldr.problem: A Dual-Stack Lite home element (B4) needs the name of its AFTR tunnel endpoint, and DHCPv6 can deliver it, but the name may live in the provider's AAA customer profile.
tldr.mechanism: A new RADIUS attribute, DS-Lite-Tunnel-Name (type 144), carries the AFTR's FQDN to the Network Access Server, which copies it into the DHCPv6 OPTION_AFTR_NAME option.
tldr.outcome: Providers can keep AFTR tunnel information in AAA profiles and still configure customers through DHCPv6. The attribute is meant for the RADIUS server and NAS, not for the B4 itself.

today: RFC 6519 is a Proposed Standard from February 2012. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why DS-Lite Needs RADIUS
sections.content:
Dual-Stack Lite (RFC 6333) offers both IPv4 and IPv6 connectivity to customers who are addressed only with an IPv6 prefix. Its key part is an IPv4-over-IPv6 tunnel. The customer's B4 element does not know whether its network supports DS-Lite, nor where the far end of the tunnel is. That far end is the AFTR (Address Family Transition Router), and its location can be given as a fully qualified domain name (FQDN).

RFC 6334 defines a DHCPv6 option the B4 uses to discover the AFTR name, but the DHCPv6 server must be pre-provisioned with that name. In broadband networks, customer profiles are often kept in AAA servers that talk RADIUS (RFC 2865) to network elements. The Network Access Server (NAS) is the access gateway and can also act as a DHCPv6 server. So a RADIUS attribute is needed to move the AFTR name from the AAA server to the NAS.
sections.eli5: The home router needs to know which helper to call. The helper's name is written in the provider's records, so the records need a way to tell the front desk.

sections.title: How RADIUS and DHCPv6 Work Together
sections.content:
The NAS is a RADIUS client and a DHCPv6 server. It sends an Access-Request to the RADIUS server, which answers with an Access-Accept holding attribute-value pairs for the session. That list MAY include the AFTR tunnel name. When the NAS gets a DHCPv6 client request containing the DS-Lite tunnel option, it SHALL use the name from the DS-Lite-Tunnel-Name attribute to fill the DHCPv6 OPTION_AFTR_NAME option in its reply.

The RFC shows two flows. With a PPP session, the NAS contacts the RADIUS server when it receives a PPP LCP Config-Request. With an IP session, the trigger is the DHCPv6 Solicit message. In the IP case the Access-Request carries a Service-Type of Authorize Only (17), so under RFC 5080 it MUST contain a State attribute.

The NAS MUST store the received name. On a DHCPv6 Renew it reuses the stored name without asking RADIUS again. On a DHCPv6 Rebind the NAS MUST send a new Access-Request, and it MAY include the attribute.
sections.eli5: The front desk asks the office for the helper's name once, writes it down, and gives it to the router. When the router asks again later, the front desk reads from its notes.

sections.title: The DS-Lite-Tunnel-Name Attribute
sections.content:
The attribute holds an FQDN naming the AFTR the client is asked to connect to. Its Type is 144. Length is the total length in octets, including the Type and Length fields. The name field is encoded as DHCPv6 requires (Section 8 of RFC 3315): a length octet for each DNS label, at most 63 octets, then the label, repeated for every label and ended by a zero-length label. The RADIUS data type is a string with opaque encapsulation.

The attribute MAY appear in Access-Request packets as a hint, for example the NAS's own default name. The server MAY ignore the hint and assign a different name. If a server does not recognize the attribute, it MUST be ignored. It MAY appear in Accounting-Request records with Acct-Status-Type Start, Stop or Interim-Update, and it MUST NOT appear more than once in a message.
sections.eli5: The name is written as a series of short labeled pieces, like spelling a web address one part at a time, with a blank piece at the end to say it is finished.

sections.title: Defaults, Changes and Failures
sections.content:
If the Access-Accept has no DS-Lite-Tunnel-Name, the NAS MAY fall back to a pre-configured default tunnel name. If it has none, or if it receives an Access-Reject, the tunnel cannot be established and the B4 has only IPv6 connectivity. If the received name differs from a configured default, the received name MUST be used. If the NAS cannot support the received name, the tunnel SHOULD NOT be established.

When an Access-Request triggered by a DHCPv6 Rebind returns a different name than the one in use, the NAS MUST force the B4 to re-establish the tunnel with the new name. If an implementation supports Change-of-Authorization messages (RFC 5176), a CoA Request containing the attribute makes the NAS send a Reconfigure message to the B4, which then does a Renew/Reply or Information-Request/Reply to get the update. A B4 that receives a different AFTR name MUST terminate its current tunnel and set up a new one.
sections.eli5: If the office gives no name, the front desk may use a backup name. If the name changes, the router hangs up on the old helper and calls the new one.

sections.title: Attribute Table, IANA and Security
sections.content:
The attribute table allows zero or one instance (0-1) in Access-Request, Access-Accept, Accounting-Request and CoA-Request, and none in Access-Reject, Access-Challenge, CoA-ACK or CoA-NACK. IANA allocated type 144 for DS-Lite-Tunnel-Name in the Radius Attribute Types registry.

There are no additional security considerations beyond those of RFC 2865 for RADIUS and RFC 5176 for CoA messages. RFC 6333 discusses security issues for Dual-Stack Lite itself.
sections.eli5: The attribute gets its own number, 144, and the rules for guarding it are the ones RADIUS already has.
